All Dec measurements are based on [turns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turn_%28angle%29#:~:text=a%20unit%20of%20plane%20angle%20measurement%20equal%20to%202%CF%80%C2%A0radians%2C%20360%C2%A0degrees). When measuring [angles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angle#:~:text=the%20figure%20formed%20by%20two%20rays)📐, a [turn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turn_%28angle%29#:~:text=the%20Greek%20letter,to%20one%20turn) ([t](#t){#turn .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="turn"}) represents a full⭕️circle and equals 360 [degrees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Degree_(angle)#:~:text=a%20measurement%20of%20a%20plane%20angle%20in%20which%20one%20full%20rotation%20is%20360%20degrees) ([°](#deg){#degree .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="degrees"}) or [$\underline\tau$](#2pi){#tau .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tau"}, 2[𝜋](#pi){#taudividedby2 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tau"}, or 900[ϡ](#sampi){#taudividedby900 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="sampi"} [radians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radian#:~:text=the%20unit%20of%20angle%20in%20the%20International%20System%20of%20Units) ([rad](#rad){#radian .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="radians"}). [Geographic coordinates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geographic_coordinate_system#:~:text=positions%20directly%20on%20Earth%20as%20latitude%20and%20longitude) and [compass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compass#:~:text=a%20device%20that%20shows%20the%20cardinal%20directions%20used%20for%20navigation%20and%20geographic%20orientation)🧭directions are angles and therefore can --- and should --- be measured in turns instead of [rad](#rad){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="radians"} or [°](#deg){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="degrees"}. # Longitude latitude course {.hiddenheading #sec-llc} Dec measures [longitude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longitude#:~:text=denoted%20by%20the%20Greek%20letter%20lambda) in [wěi](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E7%B7%AF#:~:text=(geography)-,latitude,-coordinate%20terms%C2%A0%E2%96%B2) ([w](#w){#wei .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="horizontal lines on a map"}), [latitude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latitude#:~:text=denoted%20by%20the%20Greek%20lower%2Dcase%20letter%20phi) in [jīng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meridian_arc#Full_meridian_(polar_perimeter):~:text=The%20polar%20Earth%27s%20circumference%20is%20simply%20four%20times%20quarter%20meridian) ([j](#j){#jing .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"}), and compass directions in [roses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compass_rose#:~:text=a%20polar%20diagram%20displaying%20the%20orientation%20of%20the%20cardinal%20directions)🌹([r](#r){#rose .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="roses"}). To measure certain kinds of angles, Dec uses specific types of turns with distinct names like [w](#w){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="horizontal line on a map"}, [j](#j){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"}, or [r](#r){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="rose"}. All turn types can be combined with [metric prefixes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_prefix#:~:text=a%20unit%20prefix%20that%20precedes%20a%20basic%20unit%20of%20measure%20to%20indicate%20a%20multiple%20or%20submultiple%20of%20the%20unit), like [deci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deci-#:~:text=a%20decimal%20unit%20prefix%20in%20the%20metric%20system%20denoting%20a%20factor%20of%20one%20tenth), [centi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centi-#:~:text=a%20unit%20prefix%20in%20the%20metric%20system%20denoting%20a%20factor%20of%20one%20hundredth), or [milli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milli-#:~:text=a%20unit%20prefix%20in%20the%20metric%20system%20denoting%20a%20factor%20of%20one%20thousandth), to create turn [submultiples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiple_%28mathematics%29#:~:text=of%20%22a%20being-,a%20unit%20fraction,-of%20b%22%20%28a), such as [deciturns]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tenths of a turn"} ([dt](#dt){#deciturn .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="deciturns"}), [centiturns]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hundredths of a turn"} ([ct](#ct){#centiturn .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="centiturns"}), or [milliturns]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="thousandths of a turn"} ([mt](#mt){#milliturn .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliturns"}). @tbl-map below⬇️provides the current longitude in [milliwěi]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="thousandths of a wěi"} ([mw](#mw){#milliwei .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="thousandths of a horizontal line on a map"}) and latitude in [millijīng]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="thousandths of a jīng"} ([mj](#mj){#millijing .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millijīng"}) of Points [0]{.point0} and [1]{.point1} on the [map](#fig-distmap)🗺️beneath @tbl-map. By default, Point [0]{.point0} is at [800]{.color8} [mw](#mw){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="thousandths of a horizontal line on a map"} and [0]{.color0} [mj](#mj){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millijīng"}, near the [Galápagos🏝️archipelago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gal%C3%A1pagos_Islands#:~:text=an%20archipelago%20of%20volcanic%20islands%20in%20the%20Eastern%20Pacific) of Ecuador🇪🇨, and Point [1]{.point1} is at [800]{.color8} [mw](#mw){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="thousandths of a horizontal line on a map"} and [100]{.color1} [mj](#mj){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millijīng"}, near the bottom of the [Missouri bootheel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_Bootheel#:~:text=a%20salient%20(protrusion)%20located%20in%20the%20southeasternmost%20part%20of%20the%20U.S.%20state%20of%20Missouri) in the United States🇺🇸. To move the points, click the [map](#fig-distmap) or edit their coordinates in @tbl-map. The [toggle](https://observablehq.com/framework/inputs/toggle)✅inputs above⬆️@tbl-map add layers to the [map](#fig-distmap): country borders, a rainbow🌈colored grid of Dec [graticules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graticule_(cartography)#:~:text=a%20graphical%20depiction%20of%20a%20coordinate%20system%20as%20a%20grid%20of%20lines), a [choropleth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choropleth_map#:~:text=a%20type%20of%20statistical%20thematic%20map%20that%20uses%20pseudocolor) of [Coordinated Universal Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinated_Universal_Time#:~:text=the%20primary%20time%20standard%20globally%20used%20to%20regulate%20clocks%20and%20time) ([UTC](#utc){#coordinateduniversaltime .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"}) time zones, and [solar terminator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terminator_(solar)#:~:text=a%20moving%20line%20that%20divides%20the%20daylit%20side%20and%20the%20dark%20night%20side%20of%20a%20planetary%20body) shading with a yellow🟡dot denoting the [point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subsolar_point#:~:text=the%20point%20at%20which%20its%20Sun%20is%20perceived%20to%20be%20directly%20overhead) where the Sun☀️is [directly overhead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zenith#:~:text=the%20imaginary%20point%20on%20the%20celestial%20sphere%20directly%20%22above%22%20a%20particular%20location): \${sunLonHsl} [mw](#mw){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="thousandths of a horizontal line on a map"} and \${sunLatHsl} [mj](#mj){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millijīng"}. Alongside the geographic coordinates of a point, each row of @tbl-map contains the [course](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azimuth#:~:text=%20azimuth%20is%20usually%20denoted%20alpha) in [milliroses]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="thousandths of a compass rose"} ([mr](#mr){#millirose .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliroses"}) we would need to maintain to travel🧳the shortest distance to the other point. The shortest distance is shown as orange🟠dots on the [map](#fig-distmap). The default courses in [mr](#mr){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliroses"} are [0]{.color0} (North) from Point [0]{.point0} to [1]{.point1} and [500]{.color5} (South) from Point [1]{.point1} to [0]{.point0}. # Distance speed duration {.hiddenheading #sec-dsd} Dec measures distance in [taur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turn_(angle)#Tau_proposals:~:text=%E2%81%A0%20turn-,Circumference%20of%20a%20circle,-%F0%9D%90%B6) ([c](#c){#taur .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="taur"}), speed in [omegar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angular_velocity#:~:text=linear%20velocity%20is%20the%20radius%20times%20the%20angular%20velocity) ([v](#v){#omegar .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="omegar"}), and time in years ([y](#y){#year .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="years"}) and days ([d](#d){#day .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"}). Each of these four turn types approximates ($\approx$) a physical property of the Earth🌍: [c](#c){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="taur"} = [$\underline{\tau r}$](#c){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="taur"} $\approx$ its [circumference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth%27s_circumference#:~:text=the%20distance%20around%20Earth), [y](#y){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year"} $\approx$ the duration of its [orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth%27s_orbit#:~:text=From%20a%20vantage%20point%20above%20the%20north%20pole%20of%20either%20the%20Sun%20or%20Earth%2C%20Earth%20would%20appear%20to%20revolve%20in%20a%20counterclockwise%20direction%20around%20the%20Sun) around the Sun️, [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"} $\approx$ the duration of its [rotation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth%27s_rotation#:~:text=the%20rotation%20of%20planet%20Earth%20around%20its%20own%20axis) on its [axis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axial_tilt#:~:text=the%20imaginary%20line%20that%20passes%20through%20both%20the%20north%20pole%20and%20south%20pole), and $\text c\over\text d$ = [v](#v){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="omegar"} = [$\underline{\omega r}$](#v){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="omegar"} $\approx$ the speed of its rotation at the [Equator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equator#:~:text=the%20circle%20of%20latitude%20that%20divides%20Earth%20into%20the%20Northern%20and%20Southern%20hemispheres). At a speed of [0.5]{.color5} [v](#v){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="omegar"} or [500]{.color5} [milliomegar]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="thousandths of an omegar"} ([mv](#mv){#milliomegar .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliomegar"}), we could travel the [0.1]{.color1} [c](#c){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="taur"} or [100]{.color1} [millitaur]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="thousandths of a taur"} ([mc](#mc){#millitaur .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millitaur"}) between the default positions📍of Points [0]{.point0} and [1]{.point1} in [0.2]{.color2} [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"} or [200]{.color2} [millidays]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="thousandths of a day"} ([md](#md){#milliday .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millidays"}). The time required to travel between two points is the distance divided by the speed: \${distance_mcHsl()} [mc](#mc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millitaur"} ÷ \${velocity_vHsl()} [v](#v){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="omegar"} = \${traveltimeHsl0} [md](#md){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millidays"} = \${distance_cHsl} [c](#c){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="taur"} ÷ \${velocity_vHsl()} [v](#v){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="omegar"} = \${distance_mcHsl()} [mc](#mc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millitaur"} ÷ \${velocity_mvHsl} [mv](#mv){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliomegar"} = \${traveltimeHsl1} [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"}. A box📦that is the size of a cubic [zem]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="zone equatorial meter"} ([z³](#z3){#cubiczem .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="cubic zem"}) would likely fit under a typical chair or in between the shins of two people sitting in front of each other with their knees and feet 1 [z](#z){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="zem"} apart and their legs🦵bent at right angles (25 [ct](#ct){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="centiturns"}). # Perpetually setting sun {.hiddenheading #sec-pss} In [Slovak](https://sk.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zem)🇸🇰, [zem](#z){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="zone equatorial meter"} means Earth. This is fitting because all Dec units are based on physical attributes of the Earth. At the Equator, the Earth rotates on its axis at a speed of [~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}1.00224 [v](#v){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="omegar"}. If we could indefinitely maintain this speed while flying West in an airplane✈️towards the setting sun️, we would be able to perpetually fly [into the sunset](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/RidingIntoTheSunset)🌅. # Airplane cruising speed {.hiddenheading #sec-acs} To travel fast enough for a perpetual sunset, the airplane would need to surpass the [speed of sound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speed_of_sound#:~:text=the%20distance%20travelled%20per%20unit%20of%20time%20by%20a%20sound%20wave)🔊([sos](#sos){#speedofsound .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="speed of sound"}), which at 15 [°](#deg){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="degrees"} [Celsius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celsius#:~:text=the%20unit%20of%20temperature%20on%20the%20Celsius%20temperature%20scale) and 1 [standard atmosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_atmosphere_(unit)#:~:text=a%20unit%20of%20pressure%20defined%20as%20101325%20Pa) is 0.735048 [v](#v){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="omegar"} or Mach 1. [Mach numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mach_number) are relative to the [sos](#sos){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="speed of sound"}, which varies greatly by air temperature and pressure. The cruising speed of a [Boeing 747](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_747#:~:text=sweep%2C%20allowing%20a-,Mach%C2%A00.85,-%28490%C2%A0kn;%20900) is [~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}0.54 [v](#v){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="omegar"} or Mach [~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}0.85. The highway🛣️speed of a car🚗is roughly tenfold slower than the cruising speed of an airplane️. If we are driving on a highway at a speed of 50 [mv](#mv){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliomegar"} and our exit is 1000 [z](#z){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="zem"} away, we will have 20 [centimillidays]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hundred thousandths of a day"} ([cmd](#cmd){#centimilliday .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="centimilliday"}) until we have to exit the highway️. To ensure we do not miss our exit, we can periodically check a countdown of the remaining [z](#z){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="zem"}: \${zLeft}. # Centimilliday (cmd) {.hiddenheading #sec-cmd} Dec refers to [cmd](#cmd){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="centimillidays"} as [beats]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hundred thousandths of a day"} ([b](#b){#beat .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beats"}) because they are similar in duration to heart❤️beats or [musical beats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#:~:text=I-,n%20music%20and%20music%20theory%2C%20the%20beat%20is%20the%20basic%20unit%20of%20time,-%2C%20the). In Dec, 1 [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"} = 100 [centiday]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hundredths of a day"} ([cd](#cd){#centiday .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="centidays"}) = [10^5^]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="a hundred thousand"} [b](#b){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beats"} = [10^6^]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="a million"} [microdays]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millionths of a day"} ([µd](#ud){#microday .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="microdays"}), 1 [mc](#mc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millitaur"} = 100 [kilozem]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="thousands of zem"} ([kz](#kz){#kilozem .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="thousands of zem"}) = [10^5^]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="a hundred thousand"} [z](#z){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="zem"} = [10^6^]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="a million"} [decizem]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tenths of a zem"} ([dz](#dz){#decizem .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="decizem"}) = [10^6^]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="a million"} [nanotaur]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="billionths of a taur"} ([nc](#nc){#nanotaur .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="nanotaur"}), and therefore, 1 [mv](#mv){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliomegar"} = $\text{mc}\over\text d$ = $\text {kz}\over\text {cd}$ = $\text z\over\text b$ = $\text {dz}\over\text{µd}$ = $\text {nc}\over\text{µd}$. A [cd](#cd){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="centiday"} is [96]{.color960}% of a quarter hour and a [b](#b){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beat"} is [86.4]{.color864}% of a second. # Heart rate tempo {.hiddenheading #sec-hrt} A [normal resting heart rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heart_rate#:~:text=heart%20rate%20is-,60–100%20bpm,-.%20An%20ultra%2Dtrained) is between 100 and 166.[♄]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base9 digit 6"} [b](#b){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beats"} per [md](#md){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millidays"} ([bpm](#bpm){#beatpermilliday .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beats per milliday"}). The unofficial anthem of the Dec measurement system, "[Turn the beat around](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turn_the_Beat_Around#:~:text=a%20disco%20song%20written%20by%20Gerald%20Jackson%20and%20Peter%20Jackson%2C%20and%20performed%20by%20American%20actress%20and%20singer%20Vicki%20Sue%20Robinson%20in%201976)", has a [tempo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tempo#:~:text=the%20speed%20or%20pace%20of%20a%20given%20composition) of 188.64 [bpm](#bpm){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beats per milliday"}, which corresponds to the _allegro_ [tempo marking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tempo#Approximately_from_the_slowest_to_the_fastest). A Dec clock⏰ticks at a rate of 100 [bpm](#bpm){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beats per milliday"}, $\text b^{-1}$, $1\over\text b$, 1 [inverse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiplicative_inverse#:~:text=x%2C%20denoted%20by-,1/x%20or%20x%E2%88%921,-%2C%20is%20a%20number) beat, or 1 perbeat ([þ](#per){#perbeat .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="perbeat"}), which is [1.15[♄♄]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base9 digits 6 and 6"}]{.colorIob} times more frequent than a [Hertz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hertz#:~:text=one%20event%20(or%20cycle)). # Frequency period wavelength {.hiddenheading #sec-fpw} Dec uses [þ](#per){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="perbeat"}, [b](#b){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beats"}, and [z](#z){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="zem"}, often with metric prefixes, to measure the [frequency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frequency#:~:text=the%20number%20of%20occurrences%20of%20a%20repeating%20event%20per%20unit%20of%20time), [period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frequency#:~:text=the%20reciprocal%20of%20the%20frequency), and [wavelength](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wavelength#:~:text=the%20distance%20over%20which%20the%20wave%27s%20shape%20repeats), respectively, of a sound or light wave. Equations -@eq-freq, -@eq-peri, and -@eq-wave below show how frequency, period, and wavelength are related to each other and to speed. The speed of light ([sol](#sol){#speedoflight .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="speed of light"}) is [~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}647.551657 [kiloomegar]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="thousand omegar"} ([kv](#kv){#kiloomegar .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="kiloomegar"}), which is [~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}881 thousand times faster than the [sos](#sos){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="speed of sound"}. :::{style="overflow-x:auto;overflow-y:hidden;"} $$\text{frequency} = \dfrac{\text{speed}}{\text{wavelength}} = \dfrac{1}{\text{period}}$$ {#eq-freq} $$\text{period} = \dfrac{\text{wavelength}}{\text{speed}} = \dfrac{1}{\text{frequency}}$$ {#eq-peri} $$\text{wavelength} = \text{speed} \ast \text{period} = \dfrac{\text{speed}}{\text{frequency}}$$ {#eq-wave} ::: The frequency range of the [visible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visible_spectrum#:~:text=the%20band%20of%20the%20electromagnetic%20spectrum%20that%20is%20visible%20to%20the%20human%20eye) spectrum of light is [~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}328.32 to [~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}682.56 [teraperbeats]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="trillions of perbeats"} ([Tþ](#Tpb){#teraperbeat .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="teraperbeats"}). The range of sound frequencies which can be [audible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hearing_range#:~:text=the%20frequency%20range%20that%20can%20be%20heard%20by%20humans)👂for humans is [~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}[10.368](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hearing_range#:~:text=humans%20can%20hear%20sound%20as%20low%20as%2012%C2%A0Hz) to [~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}[24192](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hearing_range#:~:text=8%5D%20and-,as%20high%20as%2028%C2%A0kHz,-%2C%20though%20the%20threshold) [þ](#per){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="perbeats"}. The period and wavelength that correspond to the frequency chosen by the range input below are 1000 ÷ \${iobs} [þ](#per){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="perbeats"} = \${parseFloat((1000 / iobs).toFixed(3))} [millibeats]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="thousandths of a beat"} ([mb](#mb){#millibeat .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millibeats"}) and 735.048 [mv](#mv){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliomegar"} ÷ \${iobs} [þ](#per){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="perbeats"} = \${parseFloat((735.048 / iobs).toFixed(3))} [z](#z){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="zem"}. ```{ojs} //| echo: false //| label: iobinput //| class: slider // https://observablehq.com/@freedmand/sounds viewof iobs = Inputs.range([1, 9999], { step: 1, value: 380, label: "Frequency" }) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false //| label: beatinput //| class: slider // https://observablehq.com/@freedmand/sounds viewof beats = Inputs.range([1, 999], { step: 1, value: 1, label: "Duration" }) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false //| label: iobplayer //| class: player // https://observablehq.com/@freedmand/sounds Play((t) => Math.sin(iobs / .864 * t * 2 * Math.PI), beats * .864, iobs) ``` # Decioctave octave note {.hiddenheading #sec-don} In addition to [þ](#per){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="perbeats"}, the limits of human hearing can also be expressed in [decioctaves]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tenths of an octave"} ([do](#do){#decioctave .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="decioctaves"}). A [do](#do){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="decioctave"} is a tenth of an [octave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octave#:~:text=an%20interval%20between%20two%20notes%2C%20one%20having%20twice%20the%20frequency%20of%20vibration%20of%20the%20other) ([o](#o){#octave .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="octave"}). An [o](#o){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="octave"} is a two-fold change in frequency. The audible range for humans is [~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}[3]{.color3} to [~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}[103]{.color3} [do](#do){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="decioctaves"}. The [range](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Range_(music)#:~:text=the%20distance%20from%20the%20lowest%20to%20the%20highest%20pitch%20it%20can%20play) of an 88-key piano🎹is [~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}23.76 to [~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}3616.64 [þ](#per){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="perbeats"} or [~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}[8]{.color8} to [~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}[80]{.color0} [do](#do){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="decioctaves"}. The equations and code below convert between [o](#o){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="octaves"} and [þ](#per){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="perbeats"}. $$\text{o} = \log_2\!\left(\frac{\text{p}}{14.1275}\right)$$ {#eq-octa} $$\text{p} = 14.1275 \ast 2^{\text{o}}$$ {#eq-perb} :::{.panel-tabset group="language"} ### Julia ::: {.cell} ```{.julia .cell-code} perbeat(o) = 14.1275 * 2.0^o ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` perbeat (generic function with 1 method) ``` ::: ```{.julia .cell-code} octave(p) = log2(p / 14.1275) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` octave (generic function with 1 method) ``` ::: ```{.julia .cell-code} octave(113.02) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 3.0 ``` ::: ```{.julia .cell-code} perbeat(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 113.02 ``` ::: ::: ### Observable JavaScript ```{ojs} perbeat = o => 14.1275 * 2 ** o; octave = p => Math.log2(p / 14.1275); octave(113.02) perbeat(3) ``` ### Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import math perbeat = lambda o: 14.1275 * 2 ** o octave = lambda p: math.log2(p / 14.1275) octave(113.02) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 3.0 ``` ::: ```{.python .cell-code} perbeat(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 113.02 ``` ::: ::: ### R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} perbeat <- \(o) 14.1275 * 2^o octave <- \(p) log2(p / 14.1275) octave(113.02) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} perbeat(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 113.02 ``` ::: ::: ::: # Color and sound {.hiddenheading #sec-cas} Each [do](#do){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="decioctave"} has a corresponding musical note ([n](#n){#note .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="musical note"}) that determines its color label. "#FFF" : "#000", xAxis: { ticks: origs.map(Math.round) }, }); } ``` # Système international d'unités {.hiddenheading #sec-sid} As a scientist of European origin, I have a strong preference for the [International System of Units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_System_of_Units#:~:text=the%20world%27s%20most%20widely%20used%20system%20of%20measurement) ([SI](#si){#internationalsystemofunits .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="International System of Units"}) over the United States🇺🇸([US](#us){#unitedstates .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="United States"}) [customary measurement system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_and_US_customary_measurement_systems). Dec units can be combined with metric prefixes to form multiples or submultiples. Dec attempts to bridge the gap, improve interoperability, and facilitate conversion between the [US](#us){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="United States"} customary and [SI](#si){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="International System of Units"} measurement systems by redefining certain units. Redefinition of [US](#us){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="United States"} customary units makes human-based length units [~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}[1.58]{.color0158}% shorter and surveying distance units [~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}[0.58]{.color0058}% shorter. Dec also redefines [SI](#si){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="International System of Units"} seconds to be [4]{.color040}% shorter. Dec color labels can convey an impression of a value at a glance👀. Dec sound labels allow us to quickly estimate a value without even having to look at it🙈. Both types of labels can help avoid confusion when [decimal separators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decimal_separator#:~:text=In%20English%2Dspeaking%20countries%2C%20the%20decimal%20point%20is%20usually%20a%20small%20dot%20%28.%29%20placed%20either%20on%20the%20baseline) appear, disappear, or move due to a measurement unit change such as the addition, removal, or replacement of a metric prefix. # Next {.unnumbered #next} Now that you have had a taste👅of Dec, I hope that you are hungry🤤for more!
